content: When a national plan designates CT scans as essential for evaluating abdominal trauma, the same principles apply as with their use in head trauma. These include ensuring prompt availability regardless of the patient’s ability to pay, maintaining the equipment in good working order with timely repairs, and implementing quality assurance monitoring. The ability to perform trauma laparotomy and manage a wide range of potential injuries to intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal structures is a cornerstone of definitive care for severely injured patients. This capability is considered essential for specialist and tertiary care hospitals, particularly where fully trained general surgeons are available. Similar to neurosurgical and thoracic trauma operations, abdominal trauma surgeries can be categorized into intermediate and advanced levels. Intermediate-level procedures include exploration, identification of injured structures, hemostasis through packing, splenectomy, hepatic packing and suturing, repair of perforated bowel, and bowel resection with anastomosis. Advanced-level procedures involve retroperitoneal surgeries, hepatic resection, and other complex interventions. General practitioner (GP) hospitals, especially in rural and low-income settings, may need to perform intermediate-level trauma laparotomies. In such settings, general practitioners often handle a variety of basic to intermediate abdominal surgical procedures, such as Caesarean sections, salpingectomy for ruptured ectopic pregnancy, repair of typhoid ileal perforations, and bowel resections for strangulated hernias. Trauma-related procedures in these circumstances may also include damage-control laparotomy before transferring the patient to higher-level facilities. When GPs are required to perform aspects of trauma laparotomy, it is critical that they possess the necessary skills to perform these procedures effectively and safely. These skills should be ensured through basic medical education and ongoing training programs. At any facility where trauma laparotomies are routinely performed, whether intermediate or advanced, the quality of these procedures must be monitored and assured through quality improvement programs. These programs should evaluate aspects such as missed injuries, delays in emergency laparotomies, and reoperation rates. Injuries to the extremities are a leading cause of trauma-related disability in many countries. Prompt recognition and correction of these injuries can significantly reduce disability. Proper immobilization of limb injuries is essential at all levels of care, as it can control hemorrhage, provide pain relief, correct deformities, and ensure safe transport. Immobilization techniques and resources, such as splints and slings, should be available even at the most basic level of care. Wrapping pelvic fractures to control hemorrhage is also essential, as it can save lives by minimizing blood loss in unstable pelvic fractures. Similarly, splinting femoral shaft fractures can reduce blood loss and provide pain relief, particularly in settings with long transportation times. Definitive management of fractures requires a range of procedures, including closed manipulation and casting, skeletal traction, external fixation (or its functional equivalent, such as pins and plaster), internal fixation, and irrigation and debridement of complex extremity wounds, including open fractures. These procedures are essential at tertiary hospitals, which typically have orthopedic surgeons. In settings where orthopedic surgeons are unavailable, general surgeons with appropriate training may need to perform these procedures, especially in areas with limited referral capabilities to tertiary facilities. The increased risk of infection with more invasive procedures, such as internal fixation, must be considered. Therefore, a sterile operating environment is essential when internal fixation is performed. In rural, low-income settings, GP-level hospitals may need to perform some definitive care procedures, including irrigation and debridement of open fractures, especially when transfers to higher-level facilities are delayed. Other procedures, such as managing hand injuries, tendon lacerations, and compartment syndrome, should also be part of the care spectrum for extremity injuries. Practitioners routinely called upon to provide care beyond their standard training should receive additional training as part of essential trauma care planning. This includes training during medical school, postgraduate programs, and continuing education courses. The availability of services implies not only the presence of necessary equipment but also the skills to use it effectively and safely. Equipment must be promptly available to all who need it, regardless of their ability to pay, and broken or worn-out equipment must be repaired or replaced. Radiographic equipment, including X-ray facilities, is essential for diagnosing and managing skeletal injuries. Portable X-rays are particularly useful for patients in traction and during operative procedures. While portable X-rays are essential at tertiary care levels, they are desirable at lower-level hospitals. C-arm image intensifiers (fluoroscopy) are increasingly integral to orthopedic care, offering accuracy, reduced operative time, decreased radiation exposure, and lower infection rates. However, cost constraints often prevent their designation as essential, though they are desirable in facilities with trained orthopedic surgeons. In countries with limited resources, non-operative treatment of fractures is often provided, even though operative repair would yield better functional outcomes. This is due to the unavailability of implants, equipment, imaging capabilities, surgical training, or a sterile operating environment, as well as patients’ inability to afford treatment. It is hoped that the benefits of early mobility through fracture stabilization will eventually be accessible to all patients who would benefit from internal or external fixation. The management of spinal injuries requires recognition of the presence or risk of such injuries at all levels of the healthcare system. This primarily requires training, including the ability to monitor neurological function at regular intervals during the acute phase of injury. Patients with spinal cord injuries, particularly acute cervical spinal cord injuries, may experience severe hypotension and ventilation difficulties. Proper management of the ABCs of trauma is critical to prevent further neurological deterioration. A holistic approach to preventing complications, such as pressure sores, urinary retention, infections, and deep vein thrombosis, is essential at all levels of care and during all phases of management, from acute care to rehabilitation. Devices for immobilization, such as spinal backboards, cervical collars, and head blocks, are essential at all hospital levels and should be used appropriately during hospital stays and inter-hospital transfers. While these devices are desirable even at basic facilities, their cost may prevent them from being designated as essential in low-volume trauma settings. However, facilities with higher trauma volumes may reasonably consider these materials essential.
